For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

derivations.claim: Write the columns of $A$ as $u,v\in\mathbb C^2$. Since $\det A=1$, $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent. Put $r_{11}:=\|u\|>0$, $q_1:=u/r_{11}$, $\alpha:=q_1^\dagger v$, $w:=v-\alpha q_1$, and $r_{22}:=\|w\|>0$. Then $q_1^\dagger w=0$ and $q_2:=w/r_{22}$ makes $Q:=(q_1,q_2)$ unitary; with $R:=\begin{pmatrix}r_{11}&\alpha\\0&r_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ we have $A=QR$. By [F1]–[F2], $1=|\det A|=|\det Q|r_{11}r_{22}=r_{11}r_{22}$, and $\det A=\det Q\,r_{11}r_{22}=1$ then gives $\det Q=1$. Therefore $Q\in SU(2)$ and $R=\begin{pmatrix}r&z\\0&r^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ for $r>0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$.

If the first column of $Q$ is $(a,c)^{\mathsf T}$, its unit orthogonal vectors are $z(-\overline c,\overline a)^{\mathsf T}$ with $|z|=1$. The determinant of the matrix with these columns is $z(|a|^2+|c|^2)=z$; $\det Q=1$ therefore forces $z=1$. Thus $Q=\begin{pmatrix}a&-\overline c\\c&\overline a\end{pmatrix}$ and $|a|^2+|c|^2=1$. This identifies $SU(2)$ with the unit sphere $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. Under this identification use the standard Euclidean inner product $\cdot$ and norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ on $\mathbb R^4$. The sphere is path-connected: non-antipodal points are joined by normalizing their straight segment. For antipodal points $x,-x\in S^3$, at least one of the first two standard basis vectors $e_1,e_2$ is not parallel to $x$; choose such an $e_j$ and set
$$w:=\frac{e_j-(e_j\cdot x)x}{\lVert e_j-(e_j\cdot x)x\rVert_2}.$$
The denominator is nonzero because $e_j$ is not parallel to $x$; hence $w\in S^3$ and $w\cdot x=0$. The normalized straight segments from $x$ to $w$ and from $w$ to $-x$ give a path. Hence there is a continuous path $Q_t$ in $SU(2)$ from $I$ to $Q$.

For $R=\begin{pmatrix}r&z\\0&r^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$, the path $R_t:=\begin{pmatrix}r^t&tz\\0&r^{-t}\end{pmatrix}$ has continuous entries because $r^{\pm t}=\exp(\pm t\log r)$ for the fixed $r>0$, and the real exponential is continuous. It has determinant one for every $t\in[0,1]$, with $R_0=I$ and $R_1=R$. Thus $A_t:=Q_tR_t$ is a continuous path in $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ from $I$ to $A=QR$. Since $A$ was arbitrary, $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ is path-connected.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

For $u\in\mathbb R^3$, set $\gamma:=\sqrt{1+|u|^2}$ and
$S:=I_3+\frac{uu^{\mathsf T}}{1+\gamma}$. Define
$B(u):=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&u^{\mathsf T}\\u&S\end{pmatrix}$. The identities
$|u|^2=\gamma^2-1$ and
$S^2=I_3+\bigl(\frac{2}{1+\gamma}+\frac{|u|^2}{(1+\gamma)^2}\bigr)uu^{\mathsf T}
=I_3+uu^{\mathsf T}$ give $B(u)^{\mathsf T}\eta B(u)=\eta$: the time-time entry is $-\gamma^2+|u|^2=-1$, the time-space block is $-\gamma u^{\mathsf T}+u^{\mathsf T}S=0$, and the spatial block is $-uu^{\mathsf T}+S^2=I_3$. Also $B(u)e_0=(\gamma,u)$ is future timelike. For $t\in[0,1]$, the entries of $B(tu)$ are continuous: $\sqrt{1+t^2|u|^2}$ is continuous and its denominator $1+\sqrt{1+t^2|u|^2}$ is positive. Thus the path $t\mapsto B(tu)$ consists of Lorentz maps and starts at the identity, so its determinant, which is always $\pm1$, stays $+1$. Each invertible Lorentz map is a homeomorphism of the timelike set and therefore maps connected components onto connected components. Since $B(tu)e_0$ lies in the future component, $B(tu)$ preserves that component by [F2]. Thus $B(u)\in SO^+(1,3)$.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, write $\Lambda e_0=(\gamma,u)$. Preservation of $\eta$ and the future cone gives $\gamma=\sqrt{1+|u|^2}>0$, so the matrix in step 1.1 satisfies $B(u)e_0=\Lambda e_0$. Then $R:=B(u)^{-1}\Lambda$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map fixing $e_0$. Its first column is $e_0$, and preservation of $\eta$ makes its first row $e_0^{\mathsf T}$; therefore $R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R_3)$ with $R_3^{\mathsf T}R_3=I_3$ and $\det R_3=1$.

The real cubic characteristic polynomial of $R_3$ has a real root, and every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of an orthogonal matrix has $|\lambda|=1$: on the complexification, $\|R_3v\|^2=v^\dagger R_3^{\mathsf T}R_3v=\|v\|^2$ for an eigenvector $v\ne0$. In particular every real eigenvalue is $+1$ or $-1$. If there were no $+1$ eigenvalue, then either all three eigenvalues would be $-1$, giving determinant $-1$, or the other two would be a conjugate pair with product $1$, again giving determinant $-1$. Both contradict $\det R_3=1$. Choose a unit eigenvector $n$ for eigenvalue $+1$. Its orthogonal plane is invariant; the restriction to that plane is orthogonal with determinant $1$, hence is a two-dimensional rotation by an angle $\theta$. Choose a unit vector $m\perp n$ and then a unit vector $p\perp n,m$ so $(n,m,p)$ is positively oriented; such $m,p$ are obtained by finite orthogonalization in the two-dimensional plane. In this basis the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. Let $C=(n,m,p)$ be the orthogonal change-of-basis matrix and denote the displayed matrix by $D(\theta)$. Then $R_3=C D(\theta)C^{\mathsf T}$, so $R_3(s):=C D(s\theta)C^{\mathsf T}$ for $s\in[0,1]$ is a continuous path in $SO(3)$ from $I_3$ to $R_3$.

Use the path $B(2tu)$ for $0\le t\le \frac12$, followed by
$B(u)\operatorname{diag}(1,R_3(2t-1))$ for $\frac12\le t\le1$, where $R_3(s)$ is the path from step 3.1. This is a continuous path in $SO^+(1,3)$ from $I_4$ to $\Lambda=B(u)R$. Hence $SO^+(1,3)$ is path-connected.

In $O(1,3)$, the determinant takes only the values $+1,-1$, so the subset with determinant $+1$ is both open and closed. The continuous map $L\mapsto Le_0$ takes $O(1,3)$ into the timelike set; by [F2], the preimage of the future timelike component is also both open and closed. Their intersection is $SO^+(1,3)$ and contains $I_4$, so the connected component of $I_4$ in $O(1,3)$ lies in $SO^+(1,3)$. Step 4.1 joins every member of $SO^+(1,3)$ to $I_4$, giving the reverse inclusion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Then there is an open
neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ of $p$ and a smooth future-directed tetrad field
$(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$
([[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]), i.e.
$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$ for all $q\in U$ with
$E_0(q)$ future-directed for every $q\in U$.

An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$. For $n>0$, a chart is oriented when its coordinate frame is in that ray. For $n=0$, the datum is a sign at each point; the unique empty frame does not encode both choices.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ and $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2,F_3)$ be two
future-directed tetrads at $p$ ([[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]).
Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Then there is a unique real
$4\times4$ matrix $\Lambda=(\Lambda^B{}_A)$ such that
$F_A=\sum_B\Lambda^B{}_AE_B$ for all $A$, and:

1. $\sum_{C,D}\Lambda^C{}_A\,\eta_{CD}\,\Lambda^D{}_B=\eta_{AB}$ for all
   $A,B$; equivalently $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$.
2. $\Lambda$ is invertible and $\det\Lambda=\pm1$.
3. $\Lambda^0{}_0>0$.
4. For every covariant $2$-tensor $T$ at $p$, its components in the two
   tetrads satisfy
   $T(F_A,F_B)=\sum_{C,D}\Lambda^C{}_A\Lambda^D{}_BT(E_C,E_D)$.
   More generally, for a type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ each contravariant slot
   contributes a factor $(\Lambda^{-1})^A{}_B$ and each covariant slot a
   factor $\Lambda^A{}_B$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: For each point $p$, use [F1] to choose a neighborhood $U$ and a smooth future-directed tetrad $E$ there. Take any coordinate chart around $p$. Relative to its coordinate determinant frame, the smooth orientation ray [F2] has locally constant sign; shrink around $p$ to keep that sign fixed, and reverse one coordinate if the sign is negative. This gives a local oriented coordinate frame. In it, the determinant of the component matrix of $E$ is a smooth nonzero real function; shrink $U$ to a connected neighborhood of $p$, so its sign is constant. If that sign is negative, replace $E_1$ by $-E_1$. This preserves orthonormality and the future direction of $E_0$ and makes $E$ positively oriented by [F2]. Thus positively oriented future tetrads exist locally.

Let $u,v$ lie in a common fiber of $P^+_g(M)$. Since $u$ is an isomorphism, $A:=u^{-1}v$ is the unique real matrix with $v=u\circ A$. The isometry condition gives $A^{\mathsf T}\eta A=\eta$. Positivity of the two frame orientations gives $\det A>0$, while the Lorentz identity gives $\det A=\pm1$, hence $\det A=1$. Because $u(e_0)$ and $v(e_0)$ are future timelike, $A e_0$ is future timelike; and the invertible Lorentz map $A$ is a homeomorphism of the timelike set. It therefore maps each connected component onto a component, and the image of $e_0$ shows that it preserves the future component. Thus $A\in SO^+(1,3)$. This proves that the right action is transitive on each fiber; uniqueness of $A$ proves freeness.

For a local positively oriented future tetrad section $E$ on $U$, define $\Psi_E:U\times SO^+(1,3)\to(P^+_g(M))|_U$ by $\Psi_E(p,A)=E(p)\circ A$. Step 1.2 makes this map bijective. Its set-theoretic inverse sends a frame $u$ over $p$ to $(p,E(p)^{-1}\circ u)$. We construct the topology and smooth structure using these bijections, rather than assuming smoothness of functions on the total space.

If $E'$ is another such section on an overlap, write $E'(p)=E(p)\circ A(p)$. Its coefficients are $A^I{}_J(p)=e^I_p(E'_J(p))$, hence are smooth functions of the base point: both $e$ and $E'$ are smooth fields on $M$. Thus $A$ is a smooth map into the embedded matrix Lie group [F4], and step 1.2 places every value in $SO^+(1,3)$. The transition between the charts is $(p,B)\mapsto(p,A(p)B)$, which is smooth; its inverse $(p,B)\mapsto(p,A(p)^{-1}B)$ is smooth because inversion is smooth in the Lie group of [F4]. Declare a subset of the total space open exactly when its preimage under every $\Psi_E$ is open. The overlap maps just computed are diffeomorphisms on open product domains, so each $\Psi_E$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset; combined with base and group coordinate charts, they give a compatible smooth atlas. In this atlas the right action is $(p,B,C)\mapsto(p,BC)$, hence smooth, and the projection is the product projection.

The charts of step 2.1 and smooth transitions from step 3.1 give $P^+_g(M)$ local products $U\times SO^+(1,3)$. Different base points separate by the Hausdorff base [F6], and distinct frames over one point separate in the Hausdorff matrix group [F4], so the total space is Hausdorff. For second countability, let $\mathcal B$ be a countable base of $M$; for each $B\in\mathcal B$ contained in at least one local-section neighborhood, use [A1] to select one pair consisting of such a neighborhood and a positively oriented future tetrad on it. The selected countable family of neighborhoods covers $M$, and countable bases of each selected $U\times SO^+(1,3)$ give a countable base of the total space by [F4,F6]. Thus the local charts define a smooth manifold structure. Freeness and fiberwise transitivity were proved in step 1.2; by [F5], this is a smooth right principal $SO^+(1,3)$-bundle. The construction supplies local sections only, so no global tetrad is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For a complex matrix $A$, write $A^\dagger:=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$. On $\mathbb C^2$ use $\langle u,v\rangle:=u^\dagger v$ and $\|u\|:=\sqrt{u^\dagger u}$, and set $SU(2):=\{Q:Q^\dagger Q=I,\det Q=1\}$. Give $M_2(\mathbb C)$ its Euclidean topology as $\mathbb R^8$, and define $SL(2,\mathbb C):=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det A=1\}$ with matrix multiplication. Then $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ is path-connected.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $\mathbb R^4$ and let
$C^+:=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:t>|x|\}$. Give
$M_4(\mathbb R)$ its Euclidean topology and define
$O(1,3):=\{L\in M_4(\mathbb R):L^{\mathsf T}\eta L=\eta\}$ with the
induced subspace topology. Define
$SO^+(1,3):=\{L\in O(1,3):\det L=1,\ L(C^+)=C^+\}$ with the same induced
topology. The **identity component** means the connected component of $I_4$
in $O(1,3)$ for this topology. Then $SO^+(1,3)$ is path-connected and equals
that identity component.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a linear map $K:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) with matrix $M$ in this basis, the following are
equivalent:

(a) $\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0$ for all $v,w\in V$;
(b) $M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M=0$;
(c) $M$ has the block form
$M=\begin{pmatrix}0&u^{T}\\ u&\Omega\end{pmatrix}$ with
$u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\Omega^{T}=-\Omega$.

The set
$\mathfrak g:=\{K:\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0\text{ for all }v,w\}$ is a
$6$-dimensional linear subspace of the space of linear maps $V\to V$. Define
the maps $M_{ab}$ for all $0\le a,b\le3$ by
$(M_{ab})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{b\nu}
-\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{a\nu}$. Thus $M_{aa}=0$ and $M_{ba}=-M_{ab}$; the six maps with $a<b$ form a basis of
$\mathfrak g$ and satisfy
$[M_{ab},M_{cd}]=\eta_{bc}M_{ad}-\eta_{ac}M_{bd}-\eta_{bd}M_{ac}
+\eta_{ad}M_{bc}$ for all $0\le a,b,c,d\le3$, where
$[K_1,K_2]:=K_1K_2-K_2K_1$ is the commutator. Here a real Lie algebra means a real vector space with a bilinear antisymmetric bracket satisfying $[K_1,[K_2,K_3]]+[K_2,[K_3,K_1]]+[K_3,[K_1,K_2]]=0$. The commutator makes $\mathfrak g$ such an algebra.
If $L:I\to O(V,\eta)$, with $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an open interval containing $0$, is a
$\mathcal C^1$ curve in $O(V,\eta)$ with $L(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$, then its
derivative $K:=L'(0)$ belongs to $\mathfrak g$, and $L(s)=\operatorname{id}_V+sK+o(s)$ as $s\to0$. Here $\mathcal C^1$ means that each matrix entry is continuously differentiable on $I$, $K$ has entries $(L^a{}_b)\prime(0)$, and $o(s)$ denotes a matrix remainder each of whose entries divided by $|s|$ tends to $0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

A **finite-dimensional real Lie group** is a group $G$, in the sense of
[[def-group]], together with the structure of a finite-dimensional real smooth
manifold such that the maps

$$m:G\times G\longrightarrow G,\qquad m(g,h)=gh,$$

and

$$\operatorname{inv}:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad \operatorname{inv}(g)=g^{-1},$$

are smooth in the sense of
[[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]. Its identity element is
denoted by $e$ (or occasionally $1$).

Unless an item explicitly says otherwise, every Lie group on this page is real,
finite-dimensional, and has no manifold boundary. Dimension zero is allowed;
for example, any countable discrete group with its discrete zero-dimensional
smooth structure is a Lie group. A Lie group cannot be empty because a group
contains its identity. The definition applies unchanged in dimension one,
uses no metric or nondegeneracy hypothesis, and makes no choice from a family
of sets.

Every Hermitian matrix has a unique form $X(x)$, since its two real diagonal entries determine $x^0,x^3$ and its complex off-diagonal entry determines $x^1,x^2$. Direct evaluation gives
$$X(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x^0+x^3&x^1-ix^2\\x^1+ix^2&x^0-x^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det X(x)=(x^0)^2-(x^1)^2-(x^2)^2-(x^3)^2.$$
Near its identity, the set $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ is a smooth real six-dimensional manifold: where the upper-left entry $a$ is nonzero, writing a matrix as $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, the equation $ad-bc=1$ uniquely gives $d=(1+bc)/a$, so $(a,b,c)$ are six real local coordinates. Left translates of this chart cover the group and have smooth transitions because left multiplication is a smooth invertible matrix map. The group product and inverse are smooth matrix operations, so [F8] makes $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ a Lie group.

For $A\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$, multiplicativity and the conjugate-transpose determinant identity in [F1] give $\det(AXA^\dagger)=\det X$. Thus the action defines a real linear Lorentz map $\rho(A)$; composition satisfies $\rho(AB)=\rho(A)\rho(B)$, and the coordinate entries are quadratic polynomials in the entries of $A$, so $\rho$ is smooth. Given any $A$, choose a path $A_t$ in $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ from $I$ to $A$ by [F2]. Then $t\mapsto\rho(A_t)$ is a path of Lorentz maps from the identity to $\rho(A)$. By [F4], its endpoint is in $SO^+(1,3)$.

A tangent matrix at $I$ to $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ has trace zero: differentiating $ad-bc=1$ at $I$ gives $Z_{11}+Z_{22}=0$. Conversely, for any trace-zero $Z=\begin{pmatrix}z&b\\c&-z\end{pmatrix}$, the curve
$$A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1+tz&tb\\tc&(1+t^2bc)/(1+tz)\end{pmatrix}$$
has determinant one near $0$ and derivative $Z$ at $0$. Hence the real tangent space has dimension six. Differentiating the action gives
$$d\rho_I(Z)X=ZX+XZ^\dagger.$$
Since [F1] shows that the action preserves $-\det X$, differentiation places $d\rho_I(Z)$ in the tangent space of the Lorentz group. If it vanishes for every Hermitian $X$, then $X=I$ gives $Z^\dagger=-Z$, and the remaining equations give $ZX=XZ$ for every Hermitian $X$. Commuting with $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ makes $Z$ diagonal; commuting with $\sigma_1$ makes its diagonal entries equal. Its trace is zero, so $Z=0$. Thus $d\rho_I$ is injective. Every tangent $K$ to $SO^+(1,3)$ at $I$ is the derivative of a smooth curve $\Lambda(t)$ in that group. Differentiating $\Lambda(t)^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda(t)=\eta$ at $t=0$ gives $K^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta K=0$, so by [F6] the target tangent lies in the six-dimensional eta-skew space. By [F5] its own dimension is six, hence it equals that space. The injective differential between the six-dimensional source and target tangent spaces is therefore an isomorphism.

Apply [F7] in smooth coordinate charts at the identity, using step 3.1: after shrinking a neighborhood $U$ of $I$ in $SL(2,\mathbb C)$, $\rho$ maps $U$ diffeomorphically onto a neighborhood $V$ of the identity in $SO^+(1,3)$. Since $\rho$ is a homomorphism, its image is a subgroup containing $V$ and hence is open. Every coset of this subgroup is open; its complement is a union of open cosets, so the image is also closed. The target is connected by [F4], and the image is nonempty, so it is all of $SO^+(1,3)$.

If $A$ lies in the kernel, then $AXA^\dagger=X$ for every Hermitian $X$. Setting $X=I$ gives $AA^\dagger=I$, so $A$ is unitary and the same equations imply $AX=XA$. Commuting with $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $\sigma_1$ as in step 3.1 forces $A=zI$; $\det A=1$ gives $z^2=1$. Both $I$ and $-I$ act trivially, hence the kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$. Shrink $U$ from step 4.1 so that $U\cap(-U)=\varnothing$. If $\rho(B)\in V$, let $C\in U$ be the unique point with $\rho(C)=\rho(B)$; then $BC^{-1}$ is in the kernel, so $B=C$ or $B=-C$. Therefore $\rho^{-1}(V)=U\sqcup(-U)$ and both pieces map diffeomorphically to $V$. Translating this neighborhood by any target element gives evenly covered neighborhoods everywhere, proving that $\rho$ is a two-sheeted covering.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let

$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies

$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention

\omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Put $c=\cosh r$ and $s=\sinh r$. Multiplying the upper-left $2\times2$ block gives
$B(r)^{\mathsf T}\eta B(r)=\eta$, because $c^2-s^2=1$ and the off-diagonal time-space terms cancel. The determinant of that block is $1$, the remaining block is identity, and $B(r)e_0=(c,s,0,0)$ is future timelike since $c>|s|$. Hence $B(r)\in SO^+(1,3)$. For the Euclidean form, however,
$\delta(B(r)e_0,B(r)e_0)=c^2+s^2>1=\delta(e_0,e_0)$ for $r\ne0$, so $B(r)\notin SO(4)$. Thus $B(r)$ is not in the image of any map with codomain $SO(4)$.

$A\sigma_1A^\dagger=\sinh r\,I+\cosh r\,\sigma_1$, and
